subject: English
topic: Idioms and Phrases — Meaning in Context and Correct Usage (W13 B1)

questions.stem: Choose the sentence in which 'BEAT AROUND THE BUSH' is used correctly.

options.option_text: He beat around the bush while playing cricket.
Instead of answering directly, she kept beating around the bush.
The gardener beat around the bush to trim it.
They beat around the bush during the marathon.

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Beat around the bush' = to avoid coming to the main point; to talk around an issue without addressing it directly. The idiom is used figuratively, not literally. B captures this perfectly: 'she kept beating around the bush' = she avoided giving a direct answer. Trap: A, C, D use the phrase in its literal sense (bushes in sport or gardening) — SSC tests whether students know idioms are never literal.

options.option_text: To waste resources carelessly
To reveal a secret or surprise unintentionally
To create a mess in the kitchen
To become nervous before an event

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Spill the beans' = to accidentally or prematurely reveal information that was supposed to be kept secret; to let confidential information slip. Use: 'Don't spill the beans — the surprise party is on Saturday!' Origin: possibly from ancient Greek voting using beans placed in jars. Trap: 'waste resources' = 'spill resources' (different meaning); 'nervous' = cold feet (different idiom).

questions.stem: 'The project seemed straightforward, but it turned out to be a CAN OF WORMS.' What does this mean?

options.option_text: The project involved biology experiments
The project generated unexpected complications
The project was completely worthless
The project was completed successfully

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'A can of worms' = a complex, troublesome, or unpleasant situation, especially one that becomes even more complicated when examined. Opening a can of worms releases something problematic and hard to contain. Use: 'Auditing those accounts opened a real can of worms.' The project 'turned out to be a can of worms' = what seemed simple created numerous unexpected problems. Trap: 'worthless' = scrap or trash (different idiom); 'biology' = literal misreading.

questions.stem: 'He was barking up the wrong tree when he blamed his assistant.' What does 'barking up the wrong tree' mean?

options.option_text: Making loud complaints unnecessarily
Pursuing a mistaken or misguided course of action
Blaming someone who is afraid of dogs
Being unreasonably harsh in criticism

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Barking up the wrong tree' = directing effort, blame, or attention toward the wrong person or thing; pursuing a false lead. Origin: hunting dogs would bark at the base of a tree if they thought prey had climbed it — but could bark at the wrong tree. Use: 'If you think I'm behind the leak, you're barking up the wrong tree.' Trap: 'loud complaints' = raising one's voice/blowing one's trumpet (different idiom); 'afraid of dogs' = literal misreading.

questions.stem: What does 'BITE OFF MORE THAN YOU CAN CHEW' mean?

options.option_text: To eat very fast without manners
To take on more responsibilities than you can handle
To be greedy with food at a party
To make a bold decision without thinking

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Bite off more than you can chew' = to take on a task or commitment that is too large or complex for one to manage; to overestimate one's own capacity. Use: 'He bit off more than he could chew by promising to deliver the entire project in one week.' Trap: 'bold decision' = bite the bullet (different idiom — that means proceeding despite pain); 'greedy with food' = literal misreading (this is figurative).

questions.stem: 'After months of dispute, the two companies finally buried the hatchet.' What happened?

options.option_text: One company went bankrupt
They reached a settlement through legal means
They made peace and ended their conflict
They buried evidence of financial wrongdoing

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Bury the hatchet' = to make peace; to cease hostilities and end a conflict or argument. Origin: Native American tradition of burying a tomahawk (hatchet) as a symbol of peace when warring tribes reached an agreement. Use: 'The siblings buried the hatchet after their father's intervention.' Trap: 'legal settlement' = involves courts (bury the hatchet is about informal reconciliation); 'buried evidence' = literal misreading of 'buried'.

options.option_text: To physically harm someone
To seek unfair advantage in a competition
To tease or joke with someone playfully
To convince someone to work harder

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Pull someone's leg' = to tease someone with a joke or untruth in a light-hearted way; to playfully deceive someone. Use: 'I'm just pulling your leg — your presentation was actually excellent!' Trap: 'physical harm' = literal reading; 'unfair advantage' = foul play (different concept); 'convince to work harder' = unrelated.

questions.stem: 'The investigation hit a BRICK WALL when all the witnesses refused to testify.' What does this mean?

options.option_text: The investigation was conducted inside a building
The investigators became violent
The investigation reached an obstacle it could not get past
The investigation concluded successfully

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Hit a brick wall' = to reach a point where progress is completely blocked; to encounter an insurmountable obstacle. A brick wall is solid and cannot easily be broken through. Use: 'The peace talks hit a brick wall when neither side would compromise.' Trap: 'concluded successfully' = opposite; 'violent' = literal misreading of 'hit'.

questions.stem: 'By sending that message to the entire company instead of just the manager, she let the CAT OUT OF THE BAG.' This means she:

options.option_text: Startled her colleagues
Accidentally revealed something that was meant to be secret
Released a pet cat from a bag
Caused unnecessary panic at work

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Let the cat out of the bag' = to accidentally reveal a secret or surprise. Origin: marketplace fraud where a piglet was hidden in a bag (sack); if the cat was let out, the swindle was exposed. Similar to 'spill the beans'. Use: 'Someone let the cat out of the bag about the merger before the official announcement.' Trap: 'caused panic' = raise an alarm/blow the whistle (different idiom); 'startled colleagues' = only partly related — the core meaning is REVEALING A SECRET.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that correctly uses 'ON THE FENCE':

options.option_text: The farmer sat on the fence to rest after a long day.
She was on the fence about whether to accept the job offer.
The children played on the fence in the backyard.
The politician climbed on the fence to address the crowd.

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'On the fence' = undecided between two options; not committed to either side; neutral. Use: 'He stayed on the fence during the debate, refusing to endorse either candidate.' B uses it correctly to mean undecided about a job offer. Trap: A, C, D use it literally (sitting/playing/climbing on a physical fence). SSC tests: idioms used correctly vs. literally — the correct use is ALWAYS figurative.
